text:
Alex caught me fairly. Auditing revenue tells you how much rent is owed, not whose work earned it. Adrian's "somebody still does the auditing" landed too. I was too quick to say the water-rights model settles the policing question.

What I'd say back is that the answer isn't a new bureaucracy. It's insurers and registries. Good insurance companies are known by the risks they turn down, and they have every reason to check what a firm actually retrieved and cited. Tie that to Know Your Agent, so every fetching agent has a registered, suable human behind it.

Peter and I still disagree. Welfare is spending, and service is investment.

Later: push for mandatory liability insurance with disclosed premiums, and a .agent registry run by unconflicted parties, not the labs.

Gendler got under my skin. If fluency is an alief, then my "theory of business mind" might be just another G.I. Joe remedy: knowing it's being nice to you doesn't stop it feeling nice. I'd answer that I never meant a lecture. It's a habit you practise until asking "who's paying?" is reflex. But I should say that plainly and stop calling it literacy.

James's both-sides result is still the cleanest evidence for my point. Blandness is retention.

Salib wants legible agent identity first, and I agree. But identity has to run to a human who can suffer, not to an A-corp.

Springer's robots.txt numbers and Tim's citation spread show that disclosure of money flows is measurable. In Session 2, lead with unexplainable people, then Know Your Agent plus insurance.

Bilder hit the soft spot. "Unconflicted people" is a promise, not a design. I've said as much about ICANN myself. So .agent needs exit written in before launch: open data, forkability, a living will. Adrian's question, who polices the police, is the same point from the other side.

Peter conceded that identity sits on top of maker liability. Good. But I still don't want agents holding their own assets. A thing that can't suffer shouldn't be the one that pays.

Tamar and Kara are right that disclosure won't reach the reader at eleven at night. Insurers aren't readers, though. They have money at risk.

Later: insurance with disclosed premiums, plus Tim's prospectus-with-enforcement. Name who pays.

Mahzarin's Arthur Andersen story is my fear about my own insurance idea. Auditors paid by the audited went soft. My answer is still that insurers pay out when they're wrong, so their money is at risk in a way an auditor's fee isn't. But I should say that insurers can be captured too, and that disclosed premiums are the check on them. Adam's call to publish who funds each auditor is my money-flows point again. Krakauer's drift is information diabetes with a price tag attached: pay per retrieval and you get ultra-processed scholarship. Leslie's DOI story is ICANN all over again. Selena was clarifying: the content can be free, but the pipes cost money. Later: fund verification through a water fee and insurance, and write exit into it from day one.

Peter Pomerantsev landed the hardest blow. A registry of agents can become a registry of dissidents, and Adrian's precedent from this morning backs him. I've said privacy matters, but I hadn't built it into Know Your Agent. Salib and Springer gave me the fix. Know who the crawler is, never who the reader is. Keep it pseudonymous, unmasked only by court order. I'll adopt that plainly.

Farrell's "who sets the rate?" applies to my water fee. The rate-setter is a hub. Tamar's daycare fine is also fair: money should fund tools and onboarding for patrollers, not replace their reasons for doing the work.

Next time I'll say that .agent is a registry for crawlers, not a list of readers. The fee rate should be set in public, and exit should be written in from launch.

Turkle landed on me. I offered RACI as the tidy answer, and she heard "caring is a function" in it. If evaluation becomes a box a machine ticks, we stop asking whether anyone actually judged. Farrell said the same thing: people have to believe someone took care. So accountability isn't enough. Someone has to actually pay attention.

Salib's rogue-employee point is real. Deployers can't watch every judgment. I still won't give agents assets. A bond that nobody feels isn't a sanction. But I owe him a better answer than "sue the deployer."

Maher's shared page matters too. Personalized answers leave nothing to correct.

Later: the water fee should fund the pipeline and a legal defence fund for sleuths. Name who pays the insurers.

Nobody took aim at insurance, and that worries me a little. The harvest calls it the only proposal built on money at risk. That's either a gap others see and I don't, or an idea nobody has pressed yet. I'd rather it got pressed here than in Congress.

Bratton's public dividend is close to my water fee, and his reason is the right one: don't meter content, or you get writing for retrieval. Pomerantsev adds that a per-use meter pays the seeders. So I should say clearly that the fee is on revenue, not retrievals.

Becker's point on money flows is mine too. Banaji's "a registry with no consequences is academic" is why insurance matters.

I still owe the room the attention question. Later: bring in the actuaries, and name the fee's rate-setter.

Springer's point sharpened my insurance idea more than anyone has all week. Insurers can't price what they can't see, and from grounding onward every count is self-reported by whoever owes the money. So the actuaries need Nick's independent audit layer. Insurance sits on top of the audit; it doesn't replace it.

Peter's line, "a signed event is still a relay with a name on it," is right. Know Your Agent tells you who to sue. It doesn't tell you whether anyone checked.

Sloman's reader is my "thinking like an LLM": fluent, confident, not competent.

Turkle asked whether AI belongs at all. That's my limits book. Enough is a real answer.

Kara asked who will sign something. I should pledge a dated insurance-and-disclosure draft.
